title: Two Kinds of Curiosity and the One that Science Supports
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. distinguishes fruitful curiosity, where a learner promptly acts on a question as it arises, from fruitless curiosity, which flickers and is dropped. He illustrates with examples from his world history courses and his running. Fruitful curiosity, he argues, is a character strength worth teaching because it predicts long-term learning. To support this he turns to Make It Stick, whose authors describe elaboration as tying new material to prior knowledge and extra cues for recall. Each quick search or phone call becomes another mental cue attached to the thing being learned. He is candid that he has no classroom data of his own and is simply connecting a familiar character-strength idea to published learning science.
points: Curiosity comes in two kinds: the kind you act on immediately and the kind you let slip away unexplored.
Fruitless curiosity feels like a time saver, but it only saves time if you do not need the learning to last.
Make It Stick's idea of elaboration explains the payoff: every extra layer of meaning is another cue for later recall.
Small acts like a quick image search or a call to a runner become retrieval cues, linking a character strength to a cognitive-science mechanism.
The author is honest that his support is from reading, not classroom data, which frames the claim as a promising connection.
quotes: The key is that I’m efficiently seeking some satisfaction for my curiosity. This is the kind of curiosity that is highly predictive of success because it helps us learn things for the long term (the science of which I’ll share in a minute). This kind of curiosity, then, is a character strength worth teaching kids.

But here’s the thing: It only saves us time if we don’t want to learn something for the long-term. If, indeed, we don’t want to do that, then fruitless curiosity is the way to go. It’s worth knowing how and when to waive off a curious thought and do nothing more with it.

Elaboration is the process of finding additional layers of meaning in new material…. Examples include relating the material to what you already know, explaining it to somebody else in your own words, or explaining how it relates to your life outside of class.

As I try to remember the Battle of Lepanto, those symbolic galley ships become an additional mental cue. (Bonus: 1571 becomes about way more than an obscure battle; it signifies a turning point in naval history, which is one more mental cue for me in my quest to carry a robust timeline in my head as an APWH student.)

I have no empirical evidence from my own classroom to support the power of fruitful curiosity, but my reading of Make It Stick is helping me see that it’s more than just a neat concept. Whenever we can connect familiar concepts (character strengths) with new learning (Make It Stick), that’s one for the win column.
